transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2026-11-18
- Start: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 62 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (BrightScale - Head of ML Infra), Priya Nair (BrightScale - SRE), Tom Anders (BrightScale - CTO)

Summary:
High-level technical deep dive focused on throughput tuning in Redwood's runtime: continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache effects, and quantization tradeoffs for a BrightScale dedicated deployment (VPC/on-prem considerations). Actionable perf test plan agreed. Some transcription artifacts and occasional mis-hearings (kvcache -> kv cash, quntization) throughout.

Topics:
- Continuous batching and scheduler behavior
- max_num_seqs and how it shapes batching vs latency
- Token limits and dynamic truncation strategies
- KV cache hits/eviction and warmup effects
- Quantization impact on throughput and memory
- VPC/on-prem networking and perf implications

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: ok thanks everyone for coming, we'll jump in, this is a throughput tuning deep dive, Samira's gonna lead on the knobs, I'm just here for context and next steps
[00:22] Samira: cool, hi, I'm Samira Patel, se on the infer team; we're gonna talk continuous batching, scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs and max_batch_size, also token limits, and kv cache warmup - forgive me if i mis-say some names, my mic's a bit echoey
[00:35] Marcus: sounds good, we mainly want to push to a 200 qps sustained target with p95 < 150ms for short chats (<=256 tokens). We have a dedicated cluster on prem in our VPC with A100s, and some nodes are older GPUs too
[01:02] Samira: perfect, that helps. quick question: what's your typical prompt distribution? seq length histogram?
[01:12] Priya: majority are short — ~60% under 128 tokens, 30% between 128-512, 10% above 512. peak arrival is spiky ecomm like 400 rps for 10-20s bursts
[01:30] Samira: good, so continuous batching will really matter for your short requests. default scheduler grouping tries to keep tail latency small by limiting max_num_seqs, but that reduces batch depth and throughput. we often recommend raising max_num_seqs to 3 or 4 for these mixed workloads, depending on p95 tolerance
[02:00] Tom: can you explain max_num_seqs again? i remember it being the number of concurrent sequences in a batch or something
[02:08] Samira: yeah, max_num_seqs is effectively how many independent sequences the scheduler will pack into a single inference wave before executing. with continuous batching, the runtime collects requests over a micro-window then issues a batched kernel. more sequences -> higher throughput but can increase single-request latency, especially if you wait to fill the bin
[02:40] Jordan: note that our continuous batching has adaptive windows - it doesn't always wait the max window, it will dispatch earlier if cpu/gpu is idle or if a latency threshold is approached
[02:56] Marcus: ok makes sense. how does token_limit interplay with that? we sometimes have very long tails with >2k tokens but low frequency
[03:10] Samira: token_limit is important. we recommend setting an effective per-request token cap for batching paths, e.g. 1k tokens for the batched pool and routing >1k tokens to a dedicated long-poll lane (or to dedicated nodes). that keeps the short-path latency tight. also consider dynamic truncation for certain prompts, or partial kv cache reuse
[03:40] Priya: when you say route to dedicated nodes, that's the dedicated pool config in Redwood Dedicated? we do have some reserved nodes we can use for long sequences
[03:48] Samira: yes, exactly — policy routing, you can mark long sequences to go to a non-batched or dedicated pool. that avoids blocking the fast path
[04:02] Jordan: one caveat is kv cache warmup. if you're splitting traffic, the KV cache locality matters. if a user has multi-turn across nodes, you lose kv hits and that increases compute. so plan your sticky routing or session affinity if multi-turn is common
[04:28] Marcus: our app is multi-turn for some flows, about 40% of sessions hit the same user across requests, can we keep kv cache warm?
[04:36] Samira: you can tune session affinity to keep a user's requests on the same worker for a TTL, but that reduces scheduling freedom. tradeoff: better kv hit-rate -> lower compute per token but lower batch packing -> slightly reduced throughput. we'll show numbers in the perf matrix
[05:05] Tom: what about quantization? we've run int8 on some local tests, got memory improvements but some degradation in output quality
[05:15] Samira: quntization (yeah apologies) — int8 and 4-bit flavors can boost token throughput and fitting bigger models onto the same GPU. but they change kernel selection and sometimes increase per-token latency for short sequences if kernels are not optimized. we prefer mixed strategy: quantize for throughput on non-latency-critical routes and use FP16 on low-latency routes where quality matters
[05:48] Marcus: are there scheduler knobs specific to quants? like prefer certain kernels or force sequence packing differently?
[05:55] Samira: we expose kernel selection flags and per-model quant profiles. we also have a quant-friendly scheduler mode that biases toward larger batches when the model is quantized because the kernel scales better with batch size. downside is p95 increases at low QPS, so careful testing required
[06:18] Jordan: re: kernels, we'll share the recommended kernel/profile mapping in the doc — different GPU generations have different sweet spots
[06:28] Samira: schedule knobs to call out: max_num_seqs, max_batch_size, micro_window_ms, late_dispatch_threshold_ms. micro_window is how long the scheduler holds requests to accumulate a batch; late_dispatch is the safety cut to avoid latency SLO violations
[06:50] Priya: what default values do you recommend for our profile? we want 200 qps sustained with occasional 400 rps bursts
[06:58] Samira: starting point: max_num_seqs=4, max_batch_size=64, micro_window_ms=15, late_dispatch_threshold_ms=30. token_limit for batched lane = 1024. these are starting values — if you need stricter p95 like <100ms we drop max_num_seqs to 2 and micro_window_ms to 8
[07:25] Marcus: that seems reasonable. can we get a chart of throughput vs p95 for those knobs?
[07:31] Samira: yes, we'll run a grid of tests and provide the CSV/spreadsheet. i'll run variants: max_num_seqs=1/2/3/4, micro_window=8/15/30ms, token_limits 512/1024/2048, and quantized vs fp16
[07:48] Tom: about kv children - sorry kv cache - how quickly does it warm after a redeploy? we've seen cold starts cause 10x cost on first minutes
[07:58] Samira: warmup depends on your session stickiness and cache eviction; for big models the KV cache loading cost is mostly in memcopy and first forward. we recommend a pre-warm step in your deployment pipeline: replay a small representative subset of recent sessions to the cluster after deploy to prepopulate caches. we can provide a small warmup script/template
[08:25] Marcus: noted, we can do that. are there metrics we should track per-route?
[08:32] Jordan: yes: tokens/sec, batch depth distribution, kv cache hit rate, micro_window fill time, per-model kernel selection, p50/p95/p99 latency, and GPU SM utilization. Redwood Console has per-route dashboards for these metrics
[08:52] Priya: networking — since we're in VPC/on-prem, are there additional latencies we should expect? we use an on-prem VPC peered to Redwood control plane, but data stays in our network via private plane
[09:06] Samira: network latency is generally minor compared to token generation but can add to tail if you have cross-region or NAT bottlenecks. for on-prem and VPC we suggest deploying the inference workers in the same L2 as your ingress and using flow-control at the edge to smooth bursts. also watch the egress to control-plane ops if you enable heavy trace sampling
[09:32] Marcus: ok, last question, how do we test the scheduler knobs in a reproducible way?
[09:40] Samira: we provide a perf harness that replays your traffic histograms with jitter and burst profiles. best practice: run 1 hour baseline with current config, then grid-run each knob change for 30m to see steady-state. collect batch depth histograms and kv hit rates. don't forget to run both cold-start and warm caches tests
[10:05] Jordan: also include a test where you isolate long sequences to dedicated nodes to validate routing policy and the effect on the fast path
[10:16] Marcus: perfect. any gotchas we've missed?
[10:20] Samira: a few small ones: 1) if you set max_num_seqs high and micro_window_ms high, you might see head-of-line blocking where a long token request prevents a batch from firing; that's why token_limit routing matters. 2) quantized kernels sometimes change memory alignment which can surface as OOM on older drivers; validate across GPU families. 3) adjust autoscaler cooldowns when you have bursty traffic else you spin up and down too quickly which warps cache locality
[10:56] Tom: brilliant. can you also share recommended defaults for our mixed GPU fleet? we have A100 and a couple of V100s
[11:05] Samira: yes, for mixed fleets prefer scheduler policy that prefers A100s for long sequences and heavier quantized loads; keep short-path traffic spread but with session affinity enabled for multi-turn. we'll annotate the spreadsheet with per-GPU recommended knobs
[11:24] Marcus: great. 
[11:29] Jordan: quick recap of next steps: Samira will run perf matrix and upload CSV + recommended config; Jordan will send the scheduler knob guide and kernel mapping; Marcus will share traffic histograms and access to a staging cluster for tests. we'll aim to have results in a week.
[11:48] Priya: noted, i'll get the histograms and a sample of session ids for warmup
[11:54] Samira: i'll include the warmup script and a sample load job, plus a patch for the session-affinity TTL tuning in the config
